name: ABC
question: Does one 100 U intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA injection reduce urgency incontinence episodes differently from a six-month oral anticholinergic regimen in women with idiopathic urgency urinary incontinence?

arms.label: OnabotulinumtoxinA 100 U intradetrusor injection with oral placebo
oral solifenacin with escalation or a switch to trospium XR, plus saline injection

design.population: 249 randomized women without neurologic disease who had five or more urgency incontinence episodes per 3-day diary, were anticholinergic-naive or had used up to two anticholinergics other than solifenacin, darifenacin or trospium, and had a postvoid residual below 150 mL.
design.description: Multicenter, double-blind, double-placebo randomized superiority trial
design.locator: PMC3543828 Methods, Study Design; Results, Participants; Figure 1

verdictNote: Episode reduction did not differ; complete resolution favored toxin, while urinary infection and catheterization were more frequent.
takeaway: In women with idiopathic urgency urinary incontinence, one 100 U onabotulinumtoxinA injection and six months of oral solifenacin (with escalation or a switch to trospium XR) reduced daily episodes similarly (3.3 versus 3.4 fewer); toxin gave more complete resolution but more urinary infection and catheterization.

reports.label: Published protocol
reports.citation: Visco AG, Brubaker L, Richter HE, et al. "Anticholinergic versus Botulinum Toxin A Comparison Trial for the Treatment of Bothersome Urge Urinary Incontinence: ABC Trial." *Contemp Clin Trials.* 2012;33(1):184-196. doi:10.1016/j.cct.2011.09.019
reports.followUp: Protocol description; no outcome data

delivery.label: Injection technique
delivery.value: Wolf injection cystoscope with the bladder filled with 100 to 200 mL; 10 mL containing 100 U onabotulinumtoxinA (or placebo) plus 0.1 mL indigo carmine injected at about 15 to 20 detrusor sites under direct vision with disposable needles, covering the posterior wall and dome and sparing the trigone, ureteral orifices and anterior dome, followed by a 1 mL saline flush.

delivery.label: Preinjection requirements
delivery.value: Negative dipstick urinalysis (below 1+ nitrite and below 1+ leukocyte) before injection; ineligible if postvoid residual was 150 mL or more on two occasions; patient or caregiver confirmed able to perform clean intermittent self-catheterization before randomization.

reports.label: Six-month randomized comparison
reports.citation: Visco AG, Brubaker L, Richter HE, et al. "Anticholinergic Therapy vs. OnabotulinumtoxinA for Urgency Urinary Incontinence." *N Engl J Med.* 2012;367(19):1803-1813. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1208872
reports.followUp: Mean change over months 1 to 6 of the double-blind phase; off-treatment follow-up to month 12

results.measure: Adjusted mean reduction in urgency incontinence episodes per day averaged over months 1 to 6 (baseline mean 5.0 per day); 241 women analyzed
results.note: Powered to detect a difference of 0.8 episodes per day (SD 2.1, 80% power, two-sided alpha 0.05 with one interim look); the report gives P only for the between-group comparison. 9% of monthly diaries were missing.

results.measure: Complete resolution of urgency incontinence among women returning at least four follow-up diaries
results.note: Secondary outcome; the report treats all analyses other than the primary as descriptive, without multiplicity adjustment.

results.measure: Complete resolution of all incontinence among women returning at least four follow-up diaries
results.note: Secondary outcome without multiplicity adjustment.

results.measure: More than 75% reduction in urgency incontinence episodes among women returning at least four follow-up diaries
results.note: Secondary outcome without multiplicity adjustment.

results.measure: Change from baseline in Overactive Bladder Questionnaire Short Form symptom-severity score (0 to 100; higher is worse), adjusted mean months 1 to 6
results.note: Secondary outcome without multiplicity adjustment.

results.measure: Change from baseline in Overactive Bladder Questionnaire Short Form quality-of-life score (0 to 100; higher is better), adjusted mean months 1 to 6
results.note: Secondary outcome without multiplicity adjustment.

results.endpoint: Adequate symptom control after treatment ended
results.measure: Adequate symptom control (Patient Global Symptom Control 4 or 5 without off-study treatment) one month after oral study drugs stopped, month 7
results.locator: PMC3543828 Results, Follow-up after cessation of treatment; Figure 3
results.note: Percentage of the 121 toxin and 126 anticholinergic participants analyzed; 85/121 (70%) and 89/126 (71%) entered off-treatment follow-up at month 6.

results.endpoint: Adequate symptom control after treatment ended
results.measure: Adequate symptom control at month 12 (six months after oral study drugs stopped)
results.locator: PMC3543828 Results, Follow-up after cessation of treatment; Figure 3
results.note: The report prints P=0.61 for this comparison.

harms.label: Urinary tract infection
harms.note: Safety population (actual treatment received), P<0.001. Infection was a urine culture above 100,000 colony-forming units per milliliter or any antibiotic course for urinary infection.

harms.label: Intermittent catheterization by study criteria at 2 months
harms.note: P=0.01. By study criteria in the toxin arm only: 10/111 (9%) at 2 weeks, 3/112 (3%) at 1 month, 3/111 (3%) at 4 months and 1/106 (1%) at 6 months; the criteria were residual above 300 mL, or above 150 mL when rated moderately or quite bothersome.

harms.label: Self-catheterization since the previous visit at 1 month
harms.note: P<0.001. Includes catheterization outside the protocol criteria; at 2 months 14/119 (12%) versus 2/122 (2%), at 4 months 11/112 (10%) versus 1/121 (1%), at 6 months 5/111 (5%) versus 1/116 (1%).

harms.label: Residual volume above 150 mL at 2 weeks
Serious adverse events
harms.note: P=0.70; the investigators attributed none of the serious adverse events to study treatment.

delivery.label: Treatment regimen
delivery.value: Solifenacin 5 mg daily, raised to 10 mg at month 2 and switched to trospium XR 60 mg at month 4 when control was inadequate and side effects tolerable, plus a saline injection; or one 100 U intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA injection plus placebo pills escalated on the same schedule.

delivery.label: Catheterization rule
delivery.value: Intermittent catheterization for postvoid residual above 300 mL, or above 150 mL when the participant rated it moderately or quite bothersome.

delivery.label: Participants and baseline severity
delivery.value: 249 randomized (127 anticholinergic, 122 toxin), 247 treated (126 and 121), 241 in the primary analysis; baseline mean 5.0 urgency incontinence episodes per day and 41% anticholinergic-naive.
delivery.note: One toxin-assigned participant received active anticholinergic with placebo injection, as treated.

reports.label: Adherence analysis
reports.citation: Visco AG, Brubaker L, Jelovsek JE, et al. "Adherence to Oral Therapy for Urgency Urinary Incontinence: Results from the Anticholinergic Versus Botox Comparison (ABC) Trial." *Female Pelvic Med Reconstr Surg.* 2016;22(1):24-28. doi:10.1097/SPV.0000000000000215
reports.followUp: Six-month double-blind phase

results.measure: Overall composite adherence (mean percentage of expected doses from pill counts and electronic cap data), toxin arm taking placebo pills versus anticholinergic arm taking active pills
results.note: Planned secondary analysis. 53% of all women were at least 80% adherent in each of the three two-month periods.

reports.label: Trial-based cost-effectiveness
reports.citation: Visco AG, Zyczynski H, Brubaker L, et al. "Cost-Effectiveness Analysis of Anticholinergics Versus Botox for Urgency Urinary Incontinence: Results From the Anticholinergic Versus Botox Comparison Randomized Trial." *Female Pelvic Med Reconstr Surg.* 2016;22(5):311-316. doi:10.1097/SPV.0000000000000277
reports.followUp: Six-month trial period; costs and symptom control modeled through 9 months

results.measure: Mean direct medical and nonmedical cost per participant over 6 months, 2012 US dollars, among 231 women completing 6 months (119 anticholinergic, 112 toxin)
results.note: Societal perspective by actual treatment received; indirect costs $106 versus $150 (P=0.62).

results.measure: Annualized quality-adjusted life-year gain from baseline (6-month utility gain times 2), derived from the OABq-SF
results.note: P compares the groups; both groups gained over baseline.

results.endpoint: Cost per month of adequate symptom control
results.measure: Modeled cumulative direct cost per month of adequate symptom control through 9 months (cumulative cost $1,266 toxin versus $1,942 anticholinergic)
results.note: Assumes no further toxin cost and sustained anticholinergic control after month 6; the oral drugs were actually stopped at 6 months in the trial.

relations.note: Both tested 100 U onabotulinumtoxinA in idiopathic overactive bladder with urgency incontinence; ABC used an anticholinergic comparator rather than placebo.

name: ALTAR
aliases: Alternative to Prophylactic Antibiotics for the Treatment of Recurrent Urinary Tract Infections in Women
question: Is methenamine hippurate noninferior to daily low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis for preventing symptomatic, antibiotic-treated urinary tract infection in women with recurrent infection?

arms.label: daily low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis (nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim or cefalexin)

design.population: 240 women with recurrent urinary tract infection (at least three episodes in 12 months or two in six months) who needed prophylaxis, recruited at eight UK secondary-care centers.
design.description: Pragmatic, multicenter, open-label noninferiority randomized trial
design.locator: BMJ full text, Abstract, Methods (Participants, Randomisation) and Results (Participants)

verdictNote: Difference of 0.49 episodes per person-year was inside the margin of 1; UTI admissions occurred only with methenamine.
takeaway: In women with recurrent urinary tract infection, methenamine hippurate was noninferior to daily low-dose nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim or cefalexin over 12 months (1.38 versus 0.89 antibiotic-treated episodes per person-year; difference 0.49, margin 1), in an open-label trial.

reports.label: 12-month randomized report (BMJ)
reports.citation: Harding C, Mossop H, Homer T, et al. "Alternative to prophylactic antibiotics for the treatment of recurrent urinary tract infections in women: multicentre, open label, randomised, non-inferiority trial." *BMJ.* 2022;376:e068229. doi:10.1136/bmj-2021-0068229
reports.followUp: 12 months of treatment plus 6 months of post-treatment follow-up; final visit January 2020

results.measure: Incidence during the 12-month treatment period, modified intention-to-treat (at least 6 months observed); episodes per person-year; absolute difference, methenamine minus antibiotics
results.note: Noninferiority margin of 1 episode per person-year (set by a patient group); met because the upper limit of the 90% CI was below 1. 95% CI for the difference 0.08 to 0.90; adjusted incidence rate ratio 1.52 (95% CI 1.16 to 1.98). Incidence 0.89 (95% CI 0.65 to 1.12) with antibiotics and 1.38 (1.05 to 1.72) with methenamine.
results.locator: BMJ full text, Results (Primary outcome), Table 2; abstract

results.measure: Prespecified sensitivity analysis, strict intention-to-treat (all randomized); episodes per person-year; absolute difference, methenamine minus antibiotics
results.note: Incidence rate ratio 1.58 (95% CI 1.24 to 2.03).

results.measure: Prespecified sensitivity analysis, per protocol (at least 90% adherence with any trial preventive treatment); episodes per person-year; absolute difference, methenamine minus antibiotics
results.note: Incidence rate ratio 1.44 (95% CI 1.02 to 2.02). Switching between strategies counted as adherent.

results.measure: Post hoc strict per-protocol analysis (at least 90% adherence with the originally allocated treatment only); episodes per person-year; absolute difference, methenamine minus antibiotics
results.note: Incidence rate ratio 1.35 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.71).

results.measure: Incidence in the 6 months after treatment; episodes per person-year; absolute difference, methenamine minus antibiotics
results.note: Incidence 1.19 (95% CI 0.86 to 1.52) with antibiotics and 1.72 (1.27 to 2.18) with methenamine.
results.locator: BMJ full text, Results (Secondary outcomes); abstract of the HTA report gives the same rates

results.measure: Incidence during the 12-month treatment period; episodes per person-year; absolute difference, methenamine minus antibiotics
results.note: Symptomatic antibiotic-treated episodes with a positive urine culture; incidence 0.41 (95% CI 0.27 to 0.56) with antibiotics and 0.53 (0.34 to 0.72) with methenamine. A urine sample accompanied 183/231 episodes (79%) and was positive in 96 (52%) of these. The confidence level of the difference is not stated in the text.

results.measure: Incidence in the 6 months after treatment; episodes per person-year; absolute difference, methenamine minus antibiotics
results.note: Incidence 0.48 (95% CI 0.28 to 0.68) with antibiotics and 0.86 (0.59 to 1.14) with methenamine. A urine sample accompanied 93/141 post-treatment episodes (66%) and was positive in 65 (70%). The confidence level of the difference is not stated in the text.

results.endpoint: Participants receiving therapeutic antibiotics for UTI
results.measure: Participants with at least one therapeutic antibiotic course for UTI during the 12-month treatment period
results.note: The text gives counts and percentages without stating the denominator. In the 6 months after treatment, median days on therapeutic antibiotics among the 52 methenamine and 48 antibiotic recipients were 13.5 (IQR 6.5 to 23) with methenamine and 7.5 (4 to 15) with antibiotics. Antibiotics for other infections: 28/98 (29%) versus 15/97 (15%).

results.measure: Participants with no UTI episode during the 12-month treatment period
results.note: Reported in the Discussion without counts or a denominator.

results.measure: Participants with E. coli (optional perineal swabs) resistant to at least one antibiotic at the 6- or 12-month visit
results.note: Chi-square test; the report calls its antimicrobial resistance analyses exploratory, with no adjustment for multiple testing. Baseline proportions were similar between groups.
results.locator: BMJ full text, Results (Antimicrobial resistance), Fig 2

results.measure: Participants with multidrug-resistant E. coli (optional perineal swabs) at month 18, six months after treatment
results.note: Fisher exact test; multidrug resistance was resistance to at least one drug in at least three antimicrobial categories.
results.locator: BMJ full text, Results (Antimicrobial resistance), Fig 2

results.measure: Urine samples with a positive culture during the 12-month treatment period (post hoc analysis)
results.note: Samples, not participants. The overall 18-month rate of asymptomatic bacteriuria was similar between groups.

results.measure: Mean treatment satisfaction questionnaire for medication convenience score (SD)
results.note: The other satisfaction domains (effectiveness, side effects, global) did not differ by arm in the report's text.

harms.label: Participants reporting an adverse reaction
harms.note: Denominators are participants receiving each treatment (analysed by treatment received, 127 and 142), not randomized arms. Most reactions were mild.

harms.label: Severe adverse event (worst grade per participant)
harms.note: By treatment received. Moderate worst-grade events: 29 (23%) versus 34 (24%).

harms.label: Serious adverse reactions
harms.locator: BMJ full text, Results (Adverse events) and Discussion
harms.note: Severe abdominal pain requiring admission and severe derangement of liver function tests, both in the antibiotic arm and classified as possibly or probably related to treatment.

harms.label: Hospital admission for UTI (18 months)
harms.locator: BMJ full text, Results (Adverse events) and Discussion
harms.note: Four participants allocated to methenamine; the Discussion states that these participants were all in the methenamine arm. Low numbers.

harms.label: Febrile UTI, temperature at least 38 degrees C (18 months)
harms.locator: BMJ full text, Results (Adverse events) and Discussion
harms.note: Six participants allocated to methenamine; the Discussion states that these participants were all in the methenamine arm.

harms.label: Nausea
harms.note: By treatment received. Only events in at least 3% of participants in either group were tabulated.

harms.label: Renal and liver function
harms.note: Blood tests every three months showed little difference in the distribution of measurements between groups or over time.

delivery.label: Regimen

values.exp: 1 g orally twice daily for 12 months
values.ctl: Once daily for 12 months: nitrofurantoin 50 or 100 mg, trimethoprim 100 mg or cefalexin 250 mg

delivery.note: The antibiotic was chosen from previous urine cultures and allergy or intolerance history.

delivery.label: Antibiotic prescribed in the antibiotic arm
delivery.value: Nitrofurantoin 66/120 (55%), trimethoprim 30/120 (25%), cefalexin 24/120 (20%).

delivery.label: Switching between strategies
delivery.note: Crossover was allowed; the primary analysis kept participants in their allocated arm.

delivery.label: At least 90% adherence

values.exp: 86 of 103 with any trial treatment; 71 with the allocated treatment only
values.ctl: 84 of 102 with any trial treatment; 82 with the allocated treatment only

delivery.note: The 86/103 and 84/102 denominators are the modified intention-to-treat arms; the strict per-protocol counts have no stated denominator.

delivery.label: Follow-up and monitoring
delivery.value: Visits every 3 months to month 18; central-laboratory urine culture at baseline, each visit and each UTI; renal and liver blood tests; optional perineal swabs at baseline and 6-monthly.

delivery.label: Verification of the primary outcome
delivery.value: Allocation of the primary outcome was verified from health records; a random sample was reviewed by a blinded independent clinician, who agreed in all cases.

reports.label: NIHR HTA monograph with economic evaluation
reports.dateLocator: Crossref and PubMed give 2022-05 only
reports.citation: Harding C, Chadwick T, Homer T, et al. "Methenamine hippurate compared with antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent recurrent urinary tract infections in women: the ALTAR non-inferiority RCT." *Health Technol Assess.* 2022;26(23):1-172. doi:10.3310/QOIZ6538
reports.followUp: 12 months of treatment plus 6 months of post-treatment observation

results.measure: Incremental cost per quality-adjusted life-year gained, Markov cohort model over the expected lifetime
results.note: The abstract states that methenamine was on average less costly and more effective in quality-adjusted life-years than antibiotics, but that this finding was not consistent over the longer term, and that progressive data loss hampered the economic evaluation. Cost and QALY values are not given in the abstract.

reports.label: Formaldehyde resistance and urine composition (PLOS Pathogens)
reports.citation: Hodgkinson NC, Al-Rubaye T, Reed TCP, et al. "Implications for methenamine hippurate use in recurrent urinary tract infection management: formaldehyde resistance and altered urinary composition." *PLoS Pathog.* 2026;22(3):e1014081. doi:10.1371/journal.ppat.1014081
reports.followUp: Retrospective laboratory analysis of stored ALTAR urines (681 samples) and 191 sequenced E. coli isolates from the 18-month trial period
reports.followUpLocator: PLOS Pathogens full text, Results (opening paragraph)

results.measure: Sequenced ALTAR E. coli isolates growing in more than 1 mM formaldehyde (11 of 191, 5.8%, from 5 participants); isolates by arm

values.ctl: 1 isolate from 1 participant (month-0 swab, before treatment)

results.note: Eight of the 11 isolates carried amino acid substitutions in the repressor FrmR and three carried plasmid-encoded frmA homologues. The per-arm isolate counts are tallied from the paper's Table 1; the paper states the 4-methenamine, 1-antibiotic split by participant. The authors describe in situ evolution in two methenamine participants over about 180 to 270 days and note that 4 of 98 methenamine participants carried resistant isolates.
results.locator: PLOS Pathogens full text, Results (Fig 2, Table 1); abstract

results.measure: HPLC components of 49 identified with higher peak area, methenamine (120 samples, 20 participants with detectable formaldehyde) versus antibiotic (55 samples, 10 participants)
results.note: Components elevated with methenamine included formaldehyde, formate and glucose. Retrospective analysis of stored urines; the authors list this as a limitation.
results.locator: PLOS Pathogens full text, Results (Urine composition), Fig 5; abstract

name: Altman (Nordic TVM)
question: Does trocar-guided anterior transvaginal polypropylene mesh repair improve one-year success over anterior colporrhaphy for symptomatic cystocele?

design.blinding: patients blinded through one year; outcome assessors unblinded

arms.label: Gynecare Prolift anterior transvaginal polypropylene mesh repair

design.population: Women aged at least 18 years with symptomatic primary or recurrent POP-Q stage 2 or higher anterior vaginal wall prolapse who did not need concomitant surgery.
design.description: Multicenter, patient-blinded superiority randomized trial
design.locator: NEJM full text, Methods: Patients, Randomization, Study Design; Figure 1

verdictNote: Composite success improved at one year, with more operative and mesh-related harms.
takeaway: Trocar-guided Gynecare Prolift anterior polypropylene mesh repair increased one-year composite anatomic and symptom success versus traditional anterior colporrhaphy (60.8% versus 34.5%); surgery was longer, bleeding and bladder perforation were more frequent, and mesh exposure required reoperation in 3.2%.

reports.label: Urodynamic substudy
reports.citation: Ek M, Tegerstedt G, Falconer C, et al. "Urodynamic assessment of anterior vaginal wall surgery: a randomized comparison between colporraphy and transvaginal mesh." *Neurourol Urodyn.* 2010;29(4):527-531. doi:10.1002/nau.20811
reports.followUp: 2 months after surgery; 50-patient randomized urodynamic substudy

results.measure: Change from baseline at 2 months in 23 mesh and 27 colporrhaphy patients
results.note: The abstract gives no numerical pressure change.

reports.label: One-year primary report
reports.citation: Altman D, Väyrynen T, Engh ME, et al. "Anterior Colporrhaphy versus Transvaginal Mesh for Pelvic-Organ Prolapse." *N Engl J Med.* 2011;364(19):1826-1836. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1009521
reports.followUp: 12 months after surgery
reports.followUpLocator: NEJM full text, Methods: Study Design; Figure 1

results.measure: One-year POP-Q anterior stage 0 or 1 plus no vaginal bulge; absolute risk difference in percentage points
results.note: Among women with evaluable composite outcomes; 200 and 189 were randomized. Adjusted OR 3.6 (95% CI 2.2–5.9); a missing-data sensitivity analysis still favored mesh.

results.measure: One-year anterior POP-Q stage 0 or 1; absolute risk difference in percentage points
One-year absence of vaginal bulge; absolute risk difference in percentage points

harms.label: New stress urinary incontinence
harms.note: P=0.05; the abstract prints 6.3% for control, but 11/176 rounds to 6.2%.

harms.label: Vaginal wound revision for mesh exposure
harms.note: All six mesh-arm wound revisions corrected exposure; P=0.03.

harms.label: Surgery for stress incontinence by 12 months
Severe pelvic pain at 2 months
harms.note: P=0.22; pain resolved by one year in all but one mesh patient.

delivery.label: Operative technique
delivery.value: Standardized Gynecare Prolift Anterior Pelvic Floor Repair System mesh kit versus standardized traditional anterior colporrhaphy; no concomitant surgery permitted.

delivery.label: Surgeon experience
delivery.value: 58 surgeons at 53 hospitals; median 3 operations of each type per surgeon.

delivery.label: Assigned treatment received
delivery.note: Nonadherence to assignment was 4.5% versus 3.7%.

delivery.label: Mean intraoperative blood loss
delivery.note: P<0.001; five mesh patients lost more than 500 mL, including one exceeding 1000 mL.

delivery.label: Perioperative measures
delivery.value: Procedures were standardized; participating surgeons were trained, and postmenopausal patients received topical estrogen before and after surgery.

reports.label: Sponsor-disclosure correction
reports.citation: "Correction: Anterior Colporrhaphy versus Transvaginal Mesh for Pelvic-Organ Prolapse." *N Engl J Med.* 2013;368(4):394. doi:10.1056/NEJMx130001
reports.followUp: No additional patient follow-up

name: ASPIRe
aliases: Apical Suspension Repair for Vault Prolapse in a Three-Arm Randomized Trial
Apical Suspension Repair for Vaginal Vault Prolapse
question: Does sacrocolpopexy or transvaginal mesh lower composite treatment failure compared with transvaginal native-tissue suspension for vault prolapse after hysterectomy, and is vaginally placed mesh noninferior to sacrocolpopexy?

design.blinding: participants masked until surgery was completed; masked personnel performed examinations and adverse event assessments from the 6-week visit
design.population: Women aged 21 or older with symptomatic vaginal vault prolapse beyond the hymen after total hysterectomy; 376 randomized, 360 treated (arm sizes are treated participants).
design.description: Nine-center, three-arm, superiority and noninferiority randomized trial
design.locator: PDF pp1-4, Figure 1; journal pp845-848

verdictNote: Sacrocolpopexy beat native tissue; mesh was noninferior to sacrocolpopexy but missed adjusted superiority over native tissue.
takeaway: Among 360 operated women with symptomatic vault prolapse after hysterectomy, sacrocolpopexy had lower modeled 36-month composite failure than transvaginal native-tissue repair (28% versus 43%); Uphold LITE transvaginal mesh (29%) was noninferior to sacrocolpopexy but not superior to native-tissue repair after multiplicity adjustment.

reports.label: 36-month randomized report
reports.citation: Menefee SA, Richter HE, Myers D, et al. Apical suspension repair for vaginal vault prolapse: a randomized clinical trial. *JAMA Surg.* 2024;159(8):845-855. doi:10.1001/jamasurg.2024.1206
reports.followUp: Analysis when the last participant reached 36 months (July 2022); 296/360 (82%) completed follow-up

results.measure: Adjusted 36-month failure probability, sacrocolpopexy versus native-tissue repair (superiority, alpha 0.01, MITT-NTR population)
results.note: Composite of retreatment for prolapse (pessary or surgery), any POP-Q measure beyond the hymen, or any bothersome bulge on the PFDI question. 95% CIs for the failure probabilities were 20%-37% and 35%-53%. Interval-censored proportional hazards model with piecewise exponential hazards, adjusted for site and age category.

results.measure: Adjusted 36-month failure probability, transvaginal mesh versus sacrocolpopexy (noninferiority, margin HR 1.93, alpha 0.03, per-protocol population)
results.note: Upper one-sided 97% confidence limit 1.65, below the 1.93 margin (the margin corresponded to a 15-point difference in 2-year failure risk, 35% versus 20%). In the modified intention-to-treat population the 36-month probabilities were 29% with transvaginal mesh and 27% with sacrocolpopexy.

results.measure: Adjusted 36-month failure probability, transvaginal mesh versus native-tissue repair (superiority, alpha 0.01, MITT-NTR population)
results.note: Did not reach the adjusted alpha of 0.01. 95% CI for the mesh failure probability 21%-38%.

results.measure: Step-down superiority test, transvaginal mesh versus sacrocolpopexy (alpha 0.03, modified intention-to-treat)
results.note: Planned after noninferiority was shown; mesh was not superior to sacrocolpopexy.

results.measure: Supportive per-protocol analysis, transvaginal mesh versus native-tissue repair
results.note: Mesh met the superiority threshold in this supportive population only; the primary population did not.

results.measure: Crude cumulative failure, modified intention-to-treat
results.note: Sacrocolpopexy denominator excludes the 2 participants switched intraoperatively to mesh (MITT-NTR population); it is 121 in the full modified intention-to-treat population.

results.measure: Retreatment (pessary or surgery) through 36 months
results.note: P across the three arms. Failure was usually anatomic only (52%-63%) or symptomatic only (27%-39%).

results.measure: Much better or very much better at 3 years
results.note: Overall P across arms.

results.measure: Mean postoperative leading edge of prolapse through 36 months, cm
results.note: Sacrocolpopexy better supported than mesh (P=0.03) and native tissue (P<0.001). Total vaginal length was longer after sacrocolpopexy than native tissue (mean difference 1.1 cm, 95% CI 0.7-1.4) and mesh (1.3 cm, 95% CI 0.9-1.6).

harms.label: Vaginal mesh exposure related to the apical procedure
harms.note: Not applicable to native-tissue repair.

harms.label: Suture exposure 12 weeks after surgery
harms.note: P=0.02. One participant each in the native-tissue and mesh arms required reoperation for vaginal exposure (suture and mesh, respectively).

harms.label: Urinary tract infection
harms.note: Overall P<0.001.

harms.label: Return to the operating room during the initial hospitalization
harms.note: Occurred only in the transvaginal mesh arm.

harms.label: Visceral organ injury and intraoperative change in surgical management
harms.note: Visceral organ injuries occurred in 3%-5% per arm without a difference among arms; intraoperative events that changed management occurred in 2%-4% per arm.

harms.label: Modified Dindo grade III or higher events and serious adverse events
harms.note: No difference among arms.

harms.label: New or worsening dyspareunia
harms.note: 9%-11% per arm among sexually active participants, without a difference among arms.

harms.label: Deaths during follow-up
harms.note: Eight deaths in total; one cardiorespiratory arrest on postoperative day 16 was judged possibly related to the intervention, the other seven occurred on postoperative days 321 to 1802 and were judged unrelated.

delivery.label: Native-tissue repair performed

values.ntr: Sacrospinous ligament fixation 110/134 (82%); uterosacral ligament suspension 24/134 (18%)

delivery.note: Both required 2 permanent and 2 delayed absorbable monofilament sutures attached to the vagina.

delivery.label: Operative time and blood loss
delivery.value: Median operative time was 90 minutes shorter in the vaginal arms than with sacrocolpopexy; blood loss was similar among arms.

delivery.label: Concomitant repairs
delivery.value: More than three-quarters of vaginal operations included anterior colporrhaphy and two-thirds included posterior colporrhaphy or perineorrhaphy; full-length midurethral slings were permitted.

delivery.label: Intraoperative conversion to the other randomized approach

values.scp: 7/129 (5%): 5 to native tissue, 2 to mesh, for intra-abdominal adhesions
values.tvm: 5/121 (4%) to native tissue: vaginal adhesions 1, cystotomy 4

delivery.note: Two further participants were switched preoperatively (1 from sacrocolpopexy and 1 from mesh to native tissue).

delivery.label: Randomization after the FDA halt on transvaginal mesh kits
delivery.value: In April 2019 the 5 participants still awaiting mesh surgery were re-randomized 1:1 to sacrocolpopexy or native tissue.

delivery.label: Examination completeness during the COVID-19 pandemic

name: ARTISAN-SNM
aliases: Axonics SacRal NeuromodulaTIon System for Urinary Urgency Incontinence TreatmeNt
question: Does single-stage implantation of the rechargeable Axonics sacral neuromodulation system, without an external test phase, reduce urgency urinary incontinence episodes in adults?

arms.label: Rechargeable Axonics sacral neuromodulation system implanted in one nonstaged procedure

design.population: Adults aged 21 or older with urgency urinary incontinence for at least 6 months (at least four leaks on a 72-hour diary, at least half associated with urgency), excluding stress or mixed incontinence, mechanical obstruction and bladder pain syndrome; 129 implanted (age 59.3 years, range 21 to 86; 98% women).
design.description: Prospective, multicenter, single-arm, unblinded pivotal study
design.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03327948 (eligibility); PMC7384085 Results, Study participants (age, sex); FDA SSED pp25, 33 (153 enrolled, 129 implanted; 15 US and 5 Western European sites)

takeaway: In 129 adults with urgency urinary incontinence, single-stage implantation of the rechargeable Axonics sacral neuromodulation system without a test phase gave 90% responders at 6 months (episodes 5.6 to 1.3 per day) and no serious device-related adverse events; there was no comparator.

results.measure: 6-month responder rate (at least 50% fewer urgency incontinence episodes on a 3-day diary), all implanted patients, as-treated

results.measure: Mean episodes per day, baseline to 6 months (mean ± SE)
ICIQ-OABqol improvement at 6 months (0 to 100 scale)
results.note: Described as clinically meaningful; FDA review: HRQL score 51.5 to 85.6, with 10 points the minimal important difference.

values.single: 13/129 (10.1%) with device-related events; 13/129 (10.1%) with procedure-related events (15 events)

harms.note: No device- or procedure-related serious events. Procedural pain was the most common procedure-related event (4 patients); implant-site pain, extremity pain and vulvovaginal pain or discomfort each occurred in 2 patients.

delivery.label: Implant technique
delivery.value: Tined lead and rechargeable neurostimulator implanted in one nonstaged procedure, without an external test phase.

name: ATLAS

question: For women seeking nonsurgical treatment of stress-predominant urinary incontinence, how do a continence pessary, behavioral therapy, and their combination compare?

design.blinding: Participants and interventionists unblinded; examination and telephone outcome assessors blinded

physician- or nurse-fitted continence ring or dish pessary

design.description: Nine-site, assessor-blinded, three-arm randomized superiority trial

verdictNote: Behavioral therapy improved symptom bother, not global improvement; combination failed its superiority rule.
takeaway: In women with stress-predominant incontinence, behavioral pelvic-floor therapy produced fewer bothersome stress symptoms than a fitted continence pessary at three months, but global improvement did not significantly differ. Adding a pessary to behavioral therapy did not meet the prespecified superiority rule.

name: Barone Fistula Catheter Trial
question: Is removing the bladder catheter 7 days after repair of a simple female genital fistula noninferior to removal at 14 days for repair breakdown?

design.population: Women at eight hospitals in eight African countries with a surgeon-judged simple genital fistula that was closed on dye test at the end of surgery and still closed 7 days after repair.

name: TVT vs PAHG
question: Is polyacrylamide hydrogel injection noninferior to retropubic tension-free vaginal tape for patient satisfaction in women with primary stress urinary incontinence?

name: Darouiche
aliases: Chlorhexidine–alcohol versus povidone–iodine for surgical-site antisepsis
question: Does preoperative skin cleansing with chlorhexidine–alcohol prevent surgical-site infection after clean-contaminated surgery better than povidone–iodine?

design.blinding: patients and infection assessors masked; operating surgeon aware once the patient was in the operating room

arms.label: Chlorhexidine–alcohol scrub (2% chlorhexidine gluconate, 70% isopropyl alcohol)

design.population: Adults undergoing clean-contaminated colorectal, small-intestinal, gastroesophageal, biliary, thoracic, gynecologic or urologic surgery at six US university-affiliated hospitals; 849 of 897 randomized patients were in the intention-to-treat analysis.
design.description: Multicenter, patient- and assessor-blinded randomized superiority trial
design.locator: PDF pp2–4, Figure 1; journal pp19–21

verdictNote: Overall and superficial incisional infection fell; deep incisional infection P=0.05; organ-space infection did not differ.
takeaway: Skin cleansing with a 2% chlorhexidine–70% isopropyl alcohol scrub lowered 30-day surgical-site infection versus aqueous 10% povidone–iodine scrub and paint after clean-contaminated surgery in 849 adults (9.5% versus 16.1%; relative risk 0.59, 95% CI 0.41–0.85).

reports.label: Initial report
reports.citation: Darouiche RO, Wall MJ Jr, Itani KMF, et al. "Chlorhexidine–Alcohol versus Povidone–Iodine for Surgical-Site Antisepsis." *N Engl J Med.* 2010;362(1):18-26. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa0810988
reports.followUp: 30 days after surgery; weekly telephone contact after discharge

results.measure: Any surgical-site infection within 30 days (CDC criteria), intention-to-treat
results.note: Fisher's exact test, two-tailed. The per-protocol analysis (813 patients) gave similar results; Kaplan–Meier freedom from infection also favored chlorhexidine–alcohol (log-rank P = 0.004).

results.measure: Superficial incisional infection within 30 days (skin and subcutaneous tissue, excluding stitch abscesses)
results.note: P values were not adjusted for multiple testing.

results.measure: Deep incisional infection within 30 days (fascia and muscle)
results.note: The relative-risk interval includes 1.

results.measure: Organ-space infection within 30 days
Sepsis from surgical-site infection within 30 days
Any surgical-site infection after abdominal (colorectal, biliary, small-intestinal, gastroesophageal) surgery; absolute difference in percentage points (chlorhexidine–alcohol minus povidone–iodine)
results.note: Subgroup analysis; the trial was not powered for subcategories. Treatment-by-surgery-type (abdominal versus nonabdominal) interaction P = 0.41. The point difference is derived by subtraction of the two percentages.

results.measure: Any surgical-site infection after nonabdominal (thoracic, gynecologic, urologic) surgery; absolute difference in percentage points (chlorhexidine–alcohol minus povidone–iodine)
results.note: Subgroup analysis; the interval includes 0. The point difference is derived by subtraction of the two percentages.

results.measure: Any surgical-site infection after urologic surgery
results.note: Descriptive counts from Table 3; no test reported. Gynecologic surgery: 0/42 versus 1/40 (2.5%); thoracic: 2/44 (4.5%) versus 4/57 (7.0%).

harms.label: Adverse events in at least 5% of patients in either group
harms.note: Absolute difference -2.4 percentage points (95% CI -9.1 to 4.2; P = 0.49).

harms.label: Serious adverse events in more than 1% of patients in either group
harms.note: Absolute difference 1.7 percentage points (95% CI -3.3 to 6.7; P = 0.52). No serious adverse event was judged related to the study preparations.

harms.label: Preparation-related adverse events (pruritus, erythema or both around the wound)
harms.note: No serious drug-related adverse events in either group, and no fire or chemical skin burn in the operating room.

harms.label: Death within 30 days
harms.note: The four deaths with chlorhexidine–alcohol occurred in patients without surgical-site infection; the three with povidone–iodine were from sepsis due to organ-space infection. P = 0.72.

delivery.note: Chlorhexidine–alcohol: scrub with an applicator containing 2% chlorhexidine gluconate and 70% isopropyl alcohol (ChloraPrep); more than one applicator was used when the area exceeded 33 by 33 cm. Povidone–iodine: scrub followed by paint with an aqueous 10% povidone–iodine solution (Scrub Care Skin Prep Tray).

name: PORTRET
aliases: Physiotherapy OR TVT Randomised Efficacy Trial
question: Does initial midurethral sling surgery improve 12-month subjective improvement over initial pelvic floor muscle physiotherapy in women with moderate-to-severe stress urinary incontinence?

arms.label: initial supervised pelvic floor muscle physiotherapy, with crossover to surgery allowed

design.population: Women aged 35 to 80 years with moderate or severe stress urinary incontinence (stress predominant if mixed) at 4 university and 19 general hospitals in the Netherlands.
design.description: Multicenter pragmatic open-label randomized superiority trial
design.locator: Methods (Study design); Results (Study population); Figure 1

verdictNote: Surgery superior at 12 months; 49.0% of the physiotherapy group crossed over to surgery.
takeaway: In women with moderate-to-severe stress urinary incontinence, initial midurethral sling surgery gave higher 12-month subjective improvement than initial pelvic floor physiotherapy (90.8% versus 64.4%) in a modified intention-to-treat analysis; 49.0% of the physiotherapy group crossed over to surgery.

reports.label: 12-month randomized report
reports.citation: Labrie J, Berghmans BL, Fischer K, et al. Surgery versus physiotherapy for stress urinary incontinence. *N Engl J Med.* 2013;369(12):1124-1133.
reports.followUp: 12 months; outcome data for 196/215 (91.2%) surgery and 174/202 (86.1%) physiotherapy women analyzed

results.measure: 12-month subjective improvement (PGI-I much or very much better); absolute difference in percentage points, surgery minus physiotherapy
results.note: Modified intention-to-treat analysis with original data; with multiple imputation the difference was 26.5 points (95% CI 18.5 to 34.2; P<0.001).
results.locator: NEJM full text, Table 2; Results (Intention-to-treat analysis)

results.measure: 12-month subjective cure (no leakage with physical activity, coughing or sneezing on the UDI item); absolute difference in percentage points
results.locator: NEJM full text, Table 2; Results (Intention-to-treat analysis)

results.measure: 12-month objective cure (negative cough stress test at bladder volume of at least 300 mL); absolute difference in percentage points
results.locator: NEJM full text, Table 2; Results (Intention-to-treat analysis)

results.measure: 12-month PGI-S no symptoms; absolute difference in percentage points
Mean change in UDI urinary incontinence domain score at 12 months (0 to 100; lower is better)
results.note: Between-group effect size 0.50 (95% CI −1.6 to 2.6), described as moderate. UDI overactive bladder domain: −15.5 (SD 20.5) versus −10.6 (SD 19.5), P=0.02.
results.locator: NEJM full text, Table 2; Results (Intention-to-treat analysis)

results.measure: 12-month PGI-I improvement, post hoc per-protocol groups: initial surgery versus physiotherapy only; absolute difference in percentage points
results.note: Post hoc analysis. Women who crossed over to surgery after physiotherapy: 86/92 (93.5%); difference from physiotherapy only 61.8 points. P<0.001 for physiotherapy only versus either surgical group; P=0.68 for surgery after physiotherapy versus initial surgery. In physiotherapy-only women, subjective cure was 13/82 (15.9%) and objective cure 33/75 (44.0%).

name: L.I.F.T.

question: Does daily D-mannose taken for 6 months reduce the proportion of women with recurrent urinary tract infection who have a further medically attended infection?

design.population: 598 women aged 18 or older (mean age 58) with at least 2 UTIs in the preceding 6 months or 3 in 12 months, recruited from 99 primary care centers in England and Wales.
design.description: Multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled superiority randomized trial

verdictNote: Not significant; the 95% CI for relative risk (0.80 to 1.05) excluded the 50% reduction the patient panel required.
takeaway: In a double-blind trial of 598 women with recurrent UTI in UK primary care, daily D-mannose 2 g for 6 months did not reduce medically attended, clinically suspected UTI versus placebo (51.0% versus 55.7%; risk difference −5 points, 95% CI −13 to 3).

reports.label: Primary report (JAMA Intern Med)

results.measure: Proportion with at least 1 further episode of clinically suspected UTI for which ambulatory care was contacted within 6 months; unadjusted risk difference, D-mannose minus placebo, in percentage points
results.note: Adjusted relative risk 0.92 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.05; P=0.22) from a log-Poisson mixed-effects model with practice as a random effect. Primary outcome data were available for 294/303 and 289/295 randomized women; the trial was powered to detect a 50% relative reduction. name: MTOPS
question: Do doxazosin, finasteride or both together delay clinical progression of BPH in men with lower urinary tract symptoms?

design.population: 3,047 men aged 50 years or older with lower urinary tract symptoms from BPH (AUA symptom score 8 to 30 or 35, maximal flow 4 to 15 mL per second) and no prior BPH treatment.
design.description: Multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled four-arm randomized trial
design.locator: NEJM PDF pp2-4, Table 1; journal pp2388-2390

verdictNote: Combination beat either drug alone; doxazosin did not reduce retention or invasive therapy.
takeaway: In 3,047 men with LUTS from BPH followed a mean of 4.5 years, doxazosin plus finasteride cut overall clinical progression risk by 66% versus placebo, more than doxazosin (39%) or finasteride (34%) alone; only finasteride and the combination significantly reduced acute retention and invasive therapy.

reports.label: Primary report (mean 4.5 years)
reports.citation: McConnell JD, Roehrborn CG, Bautista OM, et al. The long-term effect of doxazosin, finasteride, and combination therapy on the clinical progression of benign prostatic hyperplasia. *N Engl J Med.* 2003;349(25):2387-2398. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa030656
reports.followUp: Mean 4.5 years in the full-scale study (6.0 years in the 116-man pilot); 75% of men had at least 4 years of data

results.measure: Overall clinical progression, events per 100 person-years over the study (any of: confirmed AUA symptom score rise of 4 or more points, acute urinary retention, incontinence, renal insufficiency, recurrent UTI or urosepsis)
results.note: Risk reduction versus placebo (95% CI): doxazosin 39% (20 to 53; P<0.001), finasteride 34% (14 to 50; P=0.002), combination 66% (54 to 76; P<0.001); each passed the P<0.0157 threshold set for active-versus-placebo comparisons. Intention to treat; invasive BPH therapy and prostate or bladder cancer were censored as competing events.
results.locator: NEJM PDF pp3-5, Table 2; journal pp2389-2391

results.endpoint: Overall clinical progression, pairwise active comparisons
results.measure: Combination therapy versus each single drug, overall clinical progression over the study

effect.p: <0.001 for combination versus doxazosin and for combination versus finasteride

results.note: Doxazosin and finasteride did not differ significantly from each other. The protocol did not specify active-versus-active comparisons; they used a Bonferroni-adjusted threshold of P<0.0167. Number needed to treat to prevent one progression event over 4 years: 8.4 for combination, 13.7 for doxazosin, 15.0 for finasteride.

results.measure: Cumulative incidence of overall clinical progression at 4 years, among the 75% of men with at least 4 years of follow-up
results.note: P values versus placebo: doxazosin <0.001, finasteride 0.002, combination <0.001.
results.locator: NEJM PDF p4-5, Table 2; journal pp2390-2391

results.endpoint: Symptom score rise of 4 or more points
results.measure: Confirmed AUA symptom score increase of 4 or more points, events per 100 person-years
results.note: This was 78% of all progression events. Risk reduction versus placebo (95% CI): doxazosin 45% (25 to 60; P<0.001), finasteride 30% (6 to 48; P=0.016), combination 64% (48 to 75; P<0.001). Differences between finasteride and doxazosin and between combination and doxazosin were not significant.
results.locator: NEJM PDF pp4-6, Table 2; journal pp2390-2392

results.measure: Acute urinary retention, events per 100 person-years over the study

effect.p: 0.009 finasteride and <0.001 combination, each versus placebo

results.note: Risk reduction versus placebo (95% CI): doxazosin 35% (-31 to 67; cumulative incidence P=0.23), finasteride 68% (21 to 87), combination 81% (44 to 93). Four-year cumulative incidence: 2% placebo, 1% doxazosin, below 1% finasteride and combination. Retention after an obvious precipitating cause such as anesthesia counted only if a voiding trial without a catheter failed. Doxazosin delayed but did not significantly reduce retention.
results.locator: NEJM PDF pp5-7, Table 2 and Figure 2A; journal pp2391-2393

results.measure: Invasive therapy for BPH, events per 100 person-years over the study

effect.p: <0.001 for finasteride and for combination, each versus placebo

results.note: Risk reduction versus placebo (95% CI): doxazosin 3% (-48 to 37), finasteride 64% (34 to 80), combination 67% (40 to 82). Cumulative number of men with invasive therapy by year 4: 37, 26, 14 and 12 (cumulative incidence 5%, 3%, 2%, 1%). Number needed to treat to prevent one man from needing invasive therapy over 4 years: 25.9 for combination, 29.0 for finasteride, 60.1 for doxazosin. The protocol did not standardize indications for invasive therapy.
results.locator: NEJM PDF pp5-7, Table 2 and Figure 2B; journal pp2391-2393

results.measure: Mean reduction in AUA symptom score at 4 years

effect.p: <0.001 for doxazosin and combination, 0.001 for finasteride, each versus placebo over the study

results.note: Combination was superior to finasteride (P<0.001) and doxazosin (P=0.006); doxazosin was superior to finasteride (P=0.001). Median change at year 4 (Table 3): -4.0 placebo (n=534), -6.0 doxazosin (n=582), -5.0 finasteride (n=565), -7.0 combination (n=598). Secondary outcome tested with nominal P<0.05.
results.locator: NEJM PDF pp7-8, Table 3; journal pp2393-2394

results.measure: Median change in maximal urinary flow rate at 4 years, mL per second

effect.p: <0.001 for each active group versus placebo over the study

results.note: The text reports mean improvements at 4 years of 4.0 mL per second with doxazosin, 3.2 with finasteride and 5.1 with combination. Combination was superior to each single drug over the study (P<0.001 for each). Secondary outcome tested with nominal P<0.05.

name: OASIS (Revi)
question: Does an implantable tibial neuromodulation system powered by an external ankle wearable reduce urgency incontinence episodes by at least 50% in more than half of women with refractory urgency urinary incontinence?

arms.label: Revi implantable tibial neuromodulation system with an external ankle wearable

design.population: 151 implanted women (282 consented) at 23 US and European centers with urgency urinary incontinence (at least nine episodes in a 7-day diary) and an inadequate response to conservative treatment and drugs.
design.description: Prospective, multicenter, single-arm, open-label pivotal device study
design.locator: journal pp1493, 1495-1496 (Section 2, Section 3.1, Table 1)

verdictNote: Single-arm; the 6-month responder rate exceeded the prespecified 50% performance goal; no comparator group.
takeaway: In 151 women with urgency urinary incontinence in a single-arm pivotal study, the Revi implantable tibial neuromodulation system, powered by an external ankle wearable, produced a 76.4% intention-to-treat responder rate (at least 50% fewer episodes) at 6 months, above the 50% performance goal.

results.measure: Same responder definition at 12 months after activation; intention-to-treat, imputed for 12 participants with missing 12-month data

name: OPEN
aliases: Open urethroplasty versus endoscopic urethrotomy: clarifying the management of men with recurrent urethral stricture
question: In men with recurrent bulbar urethral stricture, does open urethroplasty control voiding symptoms better than endoscopic urethrotomy over 24 months?

design.blinding: open-label; central trial staff masked to allocation
design.population: 222 men with bulbar urethral stricture and at least one previous stricture operation randomized at 38 UK NHS hospitals; two ineligible men were excluded after randomization, leaving 108 and 112 by allocation.
design.description: Multicenter, open-label, patient-randomized superiority trial
design.locator: AM PDF pp5, 9, Table 1 (p18); arm counts from Table 2 (p19)

verdictNote: Symptom scores did not differ; reintervention was lower after urethroplasty; 39 of 108 urethroplasty patients lacked primary data.
takeaway: In 222 randomized UK men with recurrent bulbar urethral stricture, open urethroplasty and endoscopic urethrotomy did not differ in 24-month voiding symptom score (mean difference -0.36), but urethroplasty had fewer reinterventions (15 versus 29 men; hazard ratio 0.52, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.89).

reports.label: Primary report
reports.citation: Goulao B, Carnell S, Shen J, et al. "Surgical Treatment for Recurrent Bulbar Urethral Stricture: A Randomised Open-label Superiority Trial of Open Urethroplasty Versus Endoscopic Urethrotomy (the OPEN Trial)." *Eur Urol.* 2020;78(4):572-580. doi:10.1016/j.eururo.2020.06.003

No treatment-effect heterogeneity by time since last procedure, age, stricture length or number of previous interventions.

results.measure: Time to first reintervention (hazard ratio, urethroplasty versus urethrotomy); men with at least one reintervention

Median (IQR) interval from surgery to reintervention: 474 (399-577) days after urethroplasty versus 308 (211-448) days after urethrotomy.

results.measure: Multiple reintervention events per participant (Andersen-Gill hazard ratio)
results.note: 44 men had at least one reintervention and there were 52 reinterventions overall.

results.measure: Time to first reintervention, per-protocol analysis (men who received the allocated procedure)
results.note: Secondary analysis restricted to men who underwent the allocated procedure.

name: REACTT
aliases: A Study of Tadalafil After Radical Prostatectomy
question: Does tadalafil started early after bilateral nerve-sparing radical prostatectomy, daily or on demand, improve unassisted erectile function after the drug is stopped?

design.population: 423 men aged 68 or younger with localized prostate cancer (Gleason score 7 or lower) and normal preoperative erectile function who underwent bilateral nerve-sparing radical prostatectomy at 50 centers in nine European countries and Canada.
design.description: Multicenter, double-blind, double-dummy, placebo-controlled randomized trial

verdictNote: Unassisted recovery after washout did not improve; daily tadalafil improved drug-assisted function and penile length loss.
takeaway: In 423 men after bilateral nerve-sparing radical prostatectomy, tadalafil 5 mg daily or 20 mg on demand for 9 months did not improve unassisted erectile function after a 6-week washout versus placebo (20.9%, 16.9%, 19.1%); daily tadalafil improved drug-assisted function and reduced penile length loss.

name: RestoreX
question: Is RestoreX penile traction therapy for 30 to 90 minutes daily safe, and does it improve penile length and curvature in men with Peyronie's disease?

arms.label: RestoreX penile traction therapy for 30 to 90 minutes daily

design.population: 110 men with Peyronie's disease (diagnosed within 10 years) and curvature of 30 degrees or more, enrolled without exclusion for complex curvature, hourglass deformity, prior Peyronie's treatment or surgery, or calcification.
design.description: Single-center, single-blind (investigator) randomized controlled intent-to-treat trial; no therapy versus traction allocated 1:3

question: Does 200 U intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA reduce urgency urinary incontinence more than staged sacral neuromodulation in women with refractory symptoms?

name: UPSTREAM
aliases: Urodynamics for Prostate Surgery Trial: Randomised Evaluation of Assessment Methods
question: Does adding invasive urodynamics to routine noninvasive tests before treatment decisions for bothersome male LUTS leave symptoms no worse and reduce surgery?

design.blinding: open-label; men and hospital staff unblinded; co-applicants blinded to arm throughout recruitment and analysis, junior statistician unblinded for monitoring-committee reporting

arms.label: Routine noninvasive tests plus invasive urodynamics

design.population: 820 men (median age 68) at 26 English NHS hospitals who had received conservative or medical therapy and sought further treatment, possibly including surgery, for bothersome LUTS; catheter dependence, relevant neurologic disease, prostate or bladder cancer treatment, prior prostate surgery and unfitness for surgery were excluded.
design.description: Pragmatic multicenter open-label noninferiority randomized trial
design.locator: Eur Urol accepted manuscript PDF pp4, 6-9 and Tables PDF p2 (Table 1); CONSORT PDF p2; HTA 2020 PDF pp37, 39, 42, 50

verdictNote: IPSS noninferior at 18 months, but urodynamics did not reduce the surgery rate.
takeaway: Adding invasive urodynamics to routine noninvasive tests in men with bothersome LUTS considering prostate surgery gave an 18-month IPSS noninferior to routine tests alone (adjusted difference −0.33, 95% CI −1.47 to 0.80; margin 1 point) and did not reduce surgery (38% versus 36%).

reports.label: 18-month primary report
reports.citation: Drake MJ, Lewis AL, Young GJ, et al. "Diagnostic Assessment of Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms in Men Considering Prostate Surgery: A Noninferiority Randomised Controlled Trial of Urodynamics in 26 Hospitals." *Eur Urol.* 2020;78(5):701-710. doi:10.1016/j.eururo.2020.06.004
reports.followUp: 18 months after randomisation

results.measure: Mean IPSS at 18 months (0–35); adjusted difference, urodynamics minus routine care
results.locator: Accepted manuscript PDF pp8-9; Tables PDF p2, Table 2
results.note: Noninferiority margin 1 point, declared if the upper limit of the two-sided 95% CI was below 1 point; intention-to-treat linear regression adjusted for centre and baseline IPSS. 340 versus 329 men had an 18-month IPSS and 328 versus 313 entered the adjusted analysis (12 and 16 lacked a baseline IPSS). The IPSS fell from 18.5 (n = 403) to 12.6 with urodynamics and from 19.4 (n = 371) to 13.1 with routine care.

results.measure: Mean IPSS at 18 months, per-protocol; adjusted difference
results.locator: Accepted manuscript PDF p9; Tables PDF p2, Table 2
results.note: Men who did not receive their allocated pathway were excluded; the upper limit of 1.05 is slightly above the 1-point margin.

results.measure: Complier average causal effect on 18-month IPSS (instrumental-variable regression using allocation); adjusted difference
results.locator: Accepted manuscript PDF p9; Tables PDF p2, Table 2
results.note: 330 versus 339 men in the as-treated groups; the authors describe the result as generally similar to the intention-to-treat analysis.

results.measure: IPSS quality-of-life item at 18 months (0–6); adjusted difference, urodynamics minus routine care
results.locator: Accepted manuscript PDF p10; Tables PDF p3, Table 4
results.note: Baseline 4.1 versus 4.2; the interval excludes the 0.5-point minimal clinically important difference.

results.measure: Tests of interaction between arm and prespecified subgroups (including age and urinary function) on 18-month IPSS
results.note: No evident interactions; the authors call the tests underpowered.

results.measure: Urological surgery within 18 months
results.locator: Accepted manuscript PDF p10; Tables PDF p3, Table 3
results.note: The key secondary hypothesis was that urodynamics would reduce surgery, and the reduction was not shown; adjusted for centre, denominators are men with surgery outcome known.

results.measure: Surgery recommended by the surgeon after assessment
results.locator: Accepted manuscript PDF p10; Tables PDF p3, Table 3
results.note: Adjusted for centre. A post hoc internal validation of the recommendations against flow and urodynamic data gave 65% recommended in both as-treated arms (supplement).

results.measure: Median time from randomisation to surgery
results.note: Interquartile range 141-327 days with urodynamics and 106-284 days with routine care. In both arms at least 75% of men had TURP, the rest laser surgery, bladder neck incision, UroLift or another procedure.

results.measure: Mean maximum flow rate at 18 months (mL/s); adjusted difference
results.locator: Accepted manuscript PDF p10; Tables PDF p3, Table 3
results.note: 18 men lacked baseline data; adjusted for baseline Qmax and centre.

results.measure: Mean maximum flow rate about 4 months after surgery (mL/s) in men who had surgery; adjusted difference
results.note: One man excluded for missing baseline data.

results.measure: ICIQ-MLUTS voiding scale at 18 months; adjusted difference
ICIQ-MLUTS incontinence scale at 18 months; adjusted difference
Nocturia more than once per night at 18 months (ICIQ-MLUTS)
results.locator: Accepted manuscript PDF p10; Tables PDF p3, Table 4
results.note: The authors say it may be a chance finding given the number of secondary comparisons.

results.measure: Reduced or absent ejaculation at 18 months (ICIQ-MLUTSsex)
results.note: The authors report sexual symptoms as similar between arms and at baseline levels.

results.measure: Post hoc interaction between arm and surgery on change in IPSS
results.locator: Accepted manuscript PDF p10 (Figure 2, Supplementary Table 4)
results.note: The authors report surgery as potentially more beneficial in the routine care arm and offer delayed surgery in the urodynamics arm as one explanation. The HTA report gives p = 0.006 for the interaction between surgery and arm.

harms.label: Adverse events (all events)
harms.note: 428 events in total. No evidence that one arm was superior for adverse events per participant; related serious events were similar at event level. The slight excess in the urodynamics arm came largely from events attributed to urodynamics, for example urinary tract infection.

harms.label: Deaths within 18 months
harms.note: An independent reviewer judged none related to diagnostic testing or treatment.

delivery.label: Randomized
delivery.locator: Accepted manuscript PDF pp3, 9; CONSORT PDF p2
delivery.note: 820 men randomized 1:1 between 1 October 2014 and 31 December 2016 from 8,671 assessed; 5,910 were not eligible, 662 declined and 1,279 were not included for an unidentified reason.

delivery.label: Urodynamics received
delivery.locator: Accepted manuscript PDF p9; CONSORT PDF p2
delivery.note: Men allocated to urodynamics who did not have it: 14 declined, 14 had resolved symptoms, 10 cancelled or did not attend, 10 had an unsuccessful attempt, 3 had surgery arranged first, 17 reason missing, 6 withdrew. Routine care men who did not receive routine care only: 22 by clinician decision to use urodynamics, 2 at patient request, 2 from staff error in conducting urodynamics, 2 reason missing, 5 withdrew.

delivery.label: Withdrawals
delivery.note: 67 withdrawals, most often for poor health. The adjusted 18-month IPSS analysis included 641 men (78%): 328 (77%) with urodynamics and 313 (80%) with routine care.

delivery.label: Routine care crossovers to urodynamics
delivery.value: Mean 18-month IPSS 17.3 (n = 24) in routine care men who had urodynamics versus 12.8 (n = 305) in routine care compliers; baseline 22.6 versus 19.2.
delivery.note: The authors treat this as a small sample and note the difference was present at baseline.

delivery.label: Urodynamic quality control
delivery.value: A quality-control review found errors of standardisation, testing, interpretation and equipment maintenance, most with low risk to decisions; erroneous diagnosis of bladder outlet obstruction in 5.5% of tests.
delivery.note: Reported separately by Aiello et al., Neurourol Urodyn 2020.

delivery.label: Surgery rates below plan
delivery.value: Overall surgery rates were lower than anticipated; the design used rates from audit of local practice and surgical trials.
delivery.note: The authors attribute the lower rates to trends toward fewer surgical recommendations and acceptances during the trial and see no signal of a difference in surgery rates to suggest an underpowered study.

name: WATER
aliases: Waterjet Ablation Therapy for Endoscopic Resection of prostate tissue
question: Is robotic waterjet resection (Aquablation) noninferior to TURP for relieving BPH symptoms in men with 30 to 80 mL prostates?

design.population: Men aged 45 to 80 years with moderate-to-severe BPH-related LUTS (IPSS 12 or higher, Qmax below 15 mL/s) and a 30 to 80 mL prostate on transrectal ultrasound; 181 were treated.
design.description: Multicenter, double-blind noninferiority randomized trial
design.locator: 5-year report (Can J Urol 2022) pp10961-10963, Figure 1; arm sizes of 117 and 67 from 3-year report (Can J Urol 2020) Table 1

verdictNote: Symptom relief noninferior at 6 months; primary safety endpoint favored Aquablation (26% versus 42%).
takeaway: Aquablation, an image-guided robotic waterjet resection, was compared with TURP in men with 30 to 80 mL prostates: it was noninferior for 6-month IPSS reduction and had fewer persistent grade 1 or grade 2 or higher complications at 3 months (26% versus 42%).

reports.label: Primary report (6-month efficacy, 3-month safety)
reports.citation: Gilling P, Barber N, Bidair M, et al. "WATER: A Double-Blind, Randomized, Controlled Trial of Aquablation® vs Transurethral Resection of the Prostate in Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia." *J Urol.* 2018;199(5):1252-1261. doi:10.1016/j.juro.2017.12.065
reports.followUp: 6 months for the IPSS endpoint; 3 months for the primary safety endpoint

results.measure: Mean IPSS reduction from baseline at 6 months (Aquablation minus TURP)
results.note: Noninferiority margin 4.7 IPSS points; superiority not reached (p=0.1347). The difference is 1.8 points in favor of Aquablation.
results.locator: Abstract (noninferiority p<0.0001); means, mean difference 1.8, margin and superiority p=0.1347 in the primary report (J Urol 2018) Methods and Results; the 5-year report (Can J Urol 2022) restates the means and difference and gives superiority p=.1346; CI from FDA De Novo summary DEN170024 p12

results.measure: Clavien-Dindo persistent grade 1 or grade 2 or higher procedure-related complications at 3 months
results.note: Noninferiority met (margin 10 percentage points), then superiority tested and met (p=0.0149). Difference is Aquablation minus TURP in percentage points.
results.locator: Abstract; difference by subtraction (the Plante 2019 abstract gives the same 26% versus 42%); noninferiority margin of 10 percentage points from the 5-year report (Can J Urol 2022) p10962 and the FDA De Novo summary DEN170024

results.measure: Anejaculation among sexually active men
results.note: Sexually active men without anejaculation at baseline.

harms.label: Persistent grade 1 events at 3 months
harms.locator: 5-year report (Can J Urol 2022) p10964; restates the 3-month primary safety data
harms.note: Procedure-related anejaculation was 7% versus 25% (p=0.0004).

harms.label: Grade 2 or higher events at 3 months
harms.locator: 5-year report (Can J Urol 2022) p10964; restates the 3-month primary safety data

harms.label: Blood transfusion

harms.note: Denominators are the treated groups in the CONSORT diagram. No late bleeding event required transfusion in either arm.

harms.label: De novo erectile dysfunction or incontinence requiring a pad
harms.note: Zero events in either arm.

delivery.label: Hospital length of stay
delivery.note: Urinary catheter removed a median of 1 day after surgery in both groups.

delivery.label: Hemostasis after Aquablation
delivery.value: Focal non-resective electrocautery or low-pressure Foley balloon inflation in the prostatic fossa; continuous bladder irrigation in all patients.

reports.label: Subgroup analysis (prostate size, middle lobe, severity)

reports.followUp: 6 months for IPSS; 3 months for the primary safety endpoint

results.measure: IPSS reduction at 6 months, men with prostates 50 to 80 g (difference, Aquablation minus TURP)
results.note: Four points greater after Aquablation than after TURP, versus 1.8 points overall (p=0.135). Prespecified and post hoc exploratory subgroup analyses.

results.measure: Persistent grade 1 or grade 2 or higher complications, men with prostates 50 to 80 g
results.note: 26-point difference; overall result 26% versus 42% (p=0.015).

results.measure: IPSS change by baseline anatomy
results.note: Exploratory analysis showed larger IPSS changes after Aquablation in men with enlarged middle lobes, severe middle lobe obstruction, a low baseline maximum flow rate and a postvoid residual above 100 mL.

results.note: Reported difference 0.6 points (95% CI -3.3 to 2.2). In men with prostates of 50 cc or more, the reduction averaged 3.5 points larger after Aquablation across the 3 years (p=0.0125, repeated measures).

results.note: Median IPSS at 5 years 5.5 (Aquablation) and 6 (TURP).

name: WHO Surgical Safety Checklist
aliases: Safe Surgery Saves Lives pilot study
question: Does introducing a 19-item WHO surgical safety checklist reduce in-hospital complications and death after noncardiac surgery?

arms.label: Care after introduction of the 19-item WHO Surgical Safety Checklist
care before introduction of the checklist

design.population: Consecutive patients aged 16 or older undergoing noncardiac surgery in designated operating rooms of eight hospitals in eight cities, four in high-income and four in low- or middle-income countries.
design.description: Prospective before-and-after study at eight hospitals
design.locator: PDF pp2,4-6, Tables 2-4

verdictNote: Complications and deaths fell after implementation; prospective before-and-after design without a concurrent control group.
takeaway: In eight hospitals, introducing the WHO 19-item Surgical Safety Checklist was followed by lower in-hospital death (1.5% to 0.8%) and major complications (11.0% to 7.0%) within 30 days than care before implementation, in a prospective before-and-after study of 7,688 patients having noncardiac surgery.

reports.label: Initial report
reports.citation: Haynes AB, Weiser TG, Berry WR, et al. "A Surgical Safety Checklist to Reduce Morbidity and Mortality in a Global Population." *N Engl J Med.* 2009;360(5):491-499. doi:10.1056/NEJMsa0810119
reports.followUp: In hospital until discharge or 30 days, whichever came first

results.measure: In-hospital rate of any major complication, including death, within 30 days (site-standardized)
results.note: Difference in percentage points derived from the published rates.
results.locator: PDF p7, Table 5; PDF p6 text

results.measure: In-hospital death within 30 days (site-standardized)
results.note: No adjustment was made for multiple comparisons. Difference in percentage points derived from the published rates.
results.locator: PDF p7, Table 5; PDF p6 text

Major complications, four low- or middle-income sites

delivery.label: Checklist content
delivery.value: 19 items in three oral confirmations: sign in before induction of anesthesia, time out before skin incision, sign out before the patient leaves the operating room.

delivery.label: Introduction to the operating rooms
delivery.value: Introduced over 1 week to 1 month through local lectures, written materials or direct guidance, with a recorded video, a teleconference and a site visit from the primary investigators.

delivery.label: Study rooms
delivery.value: One to four operating rooms per hospital; consecutive patients aged 16 or older having noncardiac surgery.

delivery.label: Baseline safety practices
delivery.value: None of the eight hospitals had a formal pre- or postoperative team briefing or a standard plan for intravenous access in cases of high blood loss.

delivery.label: Sample size
delivery.value: Target of 500 consecutive patients per site per phase; calculated to detect a 20% reduction in complications with 80% power and alpha 0.05.

delivery.label: Observation by data collector
delivery.value: Operative data collected by direct observation for 37.5% of patients and from unobserved clinical teams for the rest.

delivery.label: Urgent cases
delivery.note: P=0.26. Urgent was surgery within 24 hours.
